newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook-Copper in limbo, seeks direction.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook-Copper in limbo, seeks direction.

text.p: The copper market is at a crossroads and players this week will closely eye signals of near-term direction, traders said on Monday.
Three month prices eased last week after punching up to fresh one-year highs the previous week, but seemed reluctant to explore the downside too vigorously.
The market declined by $44 last week to $2,487 per tonne, but most of the loss occurred on Monday.
The rest of the week prices moved sideways with only a half-hearted stab down to a low of $2,461, remaining just above an uptrend that began in November.
"The market is in limbo and many people are prepared to stand back," analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton said.
Chartists noted that prices were now hemmed in between the 10-day and 30-day moving averages at $2,503 and $2,442 respectively, which should provide resistance and support.
On Monday morning, prices were slightly firmer around $2,490.
Bulls regard the current weakness as a temporary correction and say there is still potential for more stock declines and tightness to hit the market.
They point to continued buying of upside call options at strikes of $2,600 to $2,700 for nearby months as evidence that some players are nervous of another surge to the upside.
But others believe reduced LME stock draws reflect reduced activity ahead of Europe's summer holiday season and before the second half, when fresh output is expected to come on line.
Last Thursday, the International Copper Study Group said it forecast a modest surplus of copper supplies this year assuming plants work at planned levels for the whole year.
In addition, selling is said to be coming out of China, the country which many bulls have counted on to go on a buying spree.
"I think the bulls pinned their hopes on rather unrealistic expectations that the Chinese would come in and absorb all of this excess production," MacMillan said.
"They are not likely to start buying at the top of the market," he added.
Aluminium ended last week $17 weaker at $1,597.
Prices finished off the $1,575 low, but some analysts believe the medium-term downtrend since mid-May is still intact.
Prices would have to close above $1,606/16 as a first sign that a bottom had been hit, analysts said.
On Monday morning, the market jumped up to $1,613 in pre-market activity.
Tin would be watched after prices surged on Friday on fund buying and borrowing in a thin market.
Prices broke above the 10-day moving average at $5,654, ending on Friday at $5,710, up $150 on the week. Last week prices hit a low of $5,510.
Lead also looked positive, gaining $15 to $642, breaching the 10-day and 30-day moving averages and nudging above a downtrend that began in August last year.
Fundamentals may be strengthening also with the approach of the replacement battery season of the summer, when demand should increase.
"A hot summer followed by a cold winter would be good for offtake," said analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff.
